title: Orchestration
subtitle: Choose a planning pattern and supply the context each step needs
summary: Pip plans a perfect museum tour; one exhibit has moved. A direct rule, an observation-driven loop, or a planner and executor may each fit different work. Pip compares useful adaptation with the calls, delay, and failure paths each pattern introduces.

concepts.title: Reflex and ReAct
concepts.body: Pip routes a known opening-hours request directly to its tool. That reflex maps input to action. For a blocked booking, ReAct interleaves planning, actions, and observations so later steps use returned facts. Pip bounds the loop: adaptive trajectories can become long and difficult to control.

concepts.title: Planner-executor
concepts.body: Pip’s planner divides a tour into rooms, timing, and access. An executor discovers that one exhibit has closed. Planner-executor separation aids clarity, debugging, and cost control, but plans can become stale. Pip reports the blocked step so planning and execution reconnect.

concepts.title: Query decomposition
concepts.body: Pip researches a new exhibition’s staffing, transport, and insurance. Query decomposition breaks the question into subquestions for iterative retrieval and synthesis. Pip reconciles dates and locations before combining the findings. More coverage brings more calls and opportunities for unsupported joins.

concepts.title: Reflection and research
concepts.body: Pip’s draft compares ticket prices from different years. A reflection step critiques the attempt and requests comparable sources. Deep research coordinates planning, tools, and synthesis; both patterns need explicit state and evaluation. Pip checks the revision against evidence because a critique can repeat an error.

misconceptions.claim: Reflex and ReAct is provided automatically by a more capable model.
misconceptions.correction: A reflex agent maps an input directly to an action. ReAct interleaves reasoning-like planning with actions and observations, allowing the next step to use tool results but potentially producing long or hard-to-control trajectories.

misconceptions.claim: Planner-executor removes the need for evaluation or human judgment.
misconceptions.correction: A planner first decomposes a task and an executor carries out steps. Separation can improve clarity, debugging, and cost control, but stale plans and coordination between phases must be handled. Evaluation and appropriate oversight remain necessary.

scenario.title: Research workflow latency
scenario.context: A research request needs several sources, but users tolerate only a few minutes.

options.label: Plan, retrieve in parallel, then synthesize with a critic
options.benefit: Improves coverage and exposes unsupported claims.
options.cost: Parallel calls and critique increase cost and orchestration complexity.
options.consequence: The critic flags a weak source before the report is delivered.

options.label: Single ReAct loop
options.benefit: Has fewer moving parts and can start immediately.
options.cost: Long trajectories and repeated searches make timing unpredictable.
options.consequence: The agent returns a plausible but incomplete report.

scenario.debrief: Both choices can fit different constraints. The decision should state stakes, reversibility, evidence, and who owns correction.

quiz.question: What distinguishes a ReAct-style loop from a plan executed without revision?
options: All tools run at the same time.
The model never sees tool results.
Reasoning and actions are interleaved with observations.
quiz.explanation: Observations can change the next step instead of relying on an unchanged initial plan.

quiz.question: A research question has several independent subquestions. What can decomposition provide?
options: Smaller searches whose results are synthesized into an answer.
A guarantee that the final synthesis contains no contradictions.
A reason to discard the original question.
quiz.explanation: Decomposition organizes work, but orchestration must still combine and check the results.

quiz.question: What is the cost of adding reflection after a draft?
options: The elimination of any need for external evidence.
Extra inference time and expense for a chance to detect problems.
A guarantee of correction at zero cost.
quiz.explanation: Reflection can improve a result but adds work and can repeat mistaken reasoning if its evidence is weak.
